extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, writers, and literate readers interested in principles of poetry and style (early-18th-century literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging heroic poems, ballads, and poetical writing that aim to move a broad public while retaining moral purpose and classical dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of Appeal / Human Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Nature is the same in all reasonable Creatures; and whatever falls in with it, will meet with Admirers amongst Readers of all Qualities and Conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that 'fall in with' common human nature will please readers of diverse backgrounds. Example: Molière's practice of reading comedies to his housekeeper and children — the audience always followed the old woman and laughed in the same places. Implication: aim for sentiments and situations that resonate with ordinary readers as well as the refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of Thought (vs. Gothick Manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential and inherent Perfection of Simplicity of Thought, above that which I call the Gothick Manner in Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity pleases all kinds of palates while the 'Gothick' or artificially fanciful manner only pleases those with an affected taste. Examples: Homer, Virgil, Milton (simple thought) vs. Martial or Cowley (epigrammatic style). Anti-pattern: over-ornamented, epigrammatic writing that delights a narrow, artificial audience but fails to move general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-audience test / Read to common folk
rubrics_metrics.description: Molière used to read all his Comedies to an old Woman ... and could foretel the Success of his Play in the Theatre from the Reception it met at his Fire-side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-elite listeners (housekeeper, children) as a test audience: if such readers respond (laugh, be moved) in the intended places, broader success is likely. This is a practical test for immediate, natural effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic Poem: Found upon a Precept of Morality adapted to the Country
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem should be founded upon some important Precept of Morality, adapted to the Constitution of the Country in which the Poet writes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poem's moral purpose should suit the nation's character and needs (Homer aimed at union among Greek states, the Chevy-Chase ballad warns against private feuds). Scoring-guidance: judge how visibly the poem promotes a pertinent moral lesson and how naturally that lesson flows from the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate Persons and Actions That Honour the Country
rubrics_metrics.description: The next Point observed by the greatest Heroic Poets, hath been to celebrate Persons and Actions which do Honour to their Country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroes and deeds that elevate national reputation; critics note Virgil's Roman hero and Homer's Greek hero as apt choices. Anti-pattern: choosing foreign or irrelevant exploits (Valerius Flaccus and Statius derided for picking the Golden Fleece/Wars of Thebes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a Hero from One's Own Country (laudable partiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet before us has not only found out an Hero in his own Country, but raises the Reputation of it by several beautiful Incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a local hero allows the poet to instill pride and present national virtues. Example devices: recounting numbers, conduct in battle, kings' reactions to enhance national esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majestic Simplicity and Naturalness in Sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments in that Ballad are extremely natural and poetical, and full of the majestick Simplicity which we admire in the greatest of the ancient Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for natural, sincere sentiments rather than artificial ornament; such simplicity evokes the majestic tone of ancient models. Example: stanzas of Chevy-Chase that resemble Virgil in spirit. Anti-pattern: contrived cleverness that undermines emotional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit for Popular Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit, it might perhaps have pleased the wrong Taste of some Readers; but it would never have become the Delight of the common People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is broad/popular appeal, do not prioritize epigram, witty conceits, or 'points' that flatter a narrow literate taste. Such devices may please critics but lose common readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Simple but Sonorous Diction ('Apparel' that suits the Thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: I must only caution the Reader not to let the Simplicity of the Stile, which one may well pardon in so old a Poet, prejudice him against the Greatness of the Thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity of language need not mean poverty of expression; sonorous numbers and suitably 'gorgeous' apparel can exist even in old or plain styles. Evaluate whether diction enhances rather than obscures the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deploy Striking, Natural Incidents to Elevate Reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ... raises the Reputation of it by several beautiful Incidents. The English are the first who take the Field, and the last who quit it ... But the most remarkable Circumstance of this kind is the different Manner in which the Scotch and English Kings receive the News of this Fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include memorable scenes and particulars (numbers at battle, kings' reactions, heroic last words) that concretely glorify characters and country. These incidents should feel natural and plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict Heroic Conduct and Moral Restraint (noble behaviour in combat)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of us two, says he, must dye: I am an Earl as well as your self ... 'tis Pity ... that so many innocent Men should perish for our sakes, rather let you and I end our Quarrel in single Fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present heroes who display honour, pity, and willingness to avoid needless slaughter (single combat, concern for innocents). Such moral restraint heightens heroism and is reminiscent of classical exempla.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Parallels and Allusion to Enrich and Legitimize
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Passage in the Eleventh Book of Virgil's Æneid ... a passage very much to be admired ... I shall take another Opportunity to consider the other Part of this old Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical parallels (e.g., Æneas/Lausus, Camilla) to situate modern scenes within a venerable tradition. These parallels can illuminate character actions and elevate the poem's moral and aesthetic weight. Take care to ensure the parallel is apt rather than forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refine Passions to Greater Elegance (transformative power of beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a third thing which may contribute ... and that is refining our Passions to a greater Elegance, than we receive them from Nature. When the Passion is Love, this Work is performed in innocent, though rude and uncultivated Minds, by the mere Force and Dignity of the Object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray love and other passions as capable of moral refinement when directed by noble objects; example: Dryden's Cymon and Iphigenia where beauty ennobles a rustic fool. As a writer, show character transformation credibly through encounters with dignified forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity via Vernacular/Real Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: But lest this fine Description should be excepted against ... I shall give my Reader, verbatim, the Epistle of an enamoured Footman ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating genuine-sounding letters, vernacular speech, or raw documents adds realism and emotional immediacy (example: James's letter). Use such materials to illustrate social types and affective states; preserve the voice's authenticity rather than over-refining it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Lasting Inward Ornaments over Transient Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to be admired ... is not to be hoped for from Beauty, or Dress, or Fashion, but from those inward Ornaments which are not to be defaced by Time or Sickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying characters (or advising real persons), emphasize virtues, intellect, and constancy rather than mere external splendour. For narrative purpose, inward qualities yield more durable admiration and moral interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Let Plain Stile Prejudice Against Great Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: I must only caution the Reader not to let the Simplicity of the Stile, which one may well pardon in so old a Poet, prejudice him against the Greatness of the Thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should evaluate the magnitude of the poet's ideas independent of a plain or archaic style; writers should not sacrifice powerful thought for ornament, nor should simple diction be dismissed as lack of genius.
